s01.text: In twenty twenty five, a research paper gave the world a number. Cache augmented generation was forty times faster than RAG. The number is real. The comparison is not.

s02.text: You have probably seen the headline. CAG is forty times faster than RAG, retrieval free, and more accurate too.

s03.text: Search that claim and you will find it repeated on LinkedIn, in engineering blogs, and in presentation slides. Almost nobody opens the paper.

s04.text: So we did. We downloaded both versions of the source, opened the tables, and read the names of the baseline rows.

s05.text: What we found is better than a misquote. The paper changed the label, and the internet kept quoting the old one.

s06.text: This is the story of a number that survived because it was repeated, not because it was read.

s07.text: First, what the two systems actually do.

s08.text: RAG stands for retrieval augmented generation. Split documents into chunks, embed them into an index, and fetch the few most relevant chunks for each question.

s09.text: The model sees those chunks and the question. It never sees the whole knowledge base. Its answer can only be as good as the chunks that were fetched.

s10.text: CAG takes the opposite bet. Cache augmented generation preloads the entire curated corpus into the context window once.

s11.text: The model reads it, computes the key and value tensors for every token, and saves that state. The saved state is the K V cache.

s12.text: When a question arrives, only the question is processed. The corpus is already there. No retrieval step, no embedding lookup, no ranking.

s13.text: After the answer, the extra question tokens are trimmed and the cache returns to its clean state.

s14.text: That is a clever idea. It removes a whole class of failures: the right document never being retrieved at all.

s15.text: But notice what the cache does not remove. The model still attends over every token in that corpus for every token it generates.

s16.text: The cache saves the reading. It does not save the thinking.

s17.text: So how was the forty times figure produced? The authors tested Llama three point one, eight billion parameters, on two question answering benchmarks.

s18.text: S QuAD, where the answer sits in one passage, and Hot Pot Q A, where you must connect facts across documents.

s19.text: They built three corpus sizes. Sixteen, thirty two, and sixty four documents, from twenty one thousand up to eighty five thousand tokens.

s20.text: The largest set is the interesting one. Sixty four documents, eighty five thousand tokens, and one thousand three hundred forty four questions.

s21.text: They ran sparse BM twenty five retrieval, dense vector retrieval, plain long context with no cache, and their cached method.

s22.text: Every system used the same model. The hardware was eight Tesla V one hundred GPUs.

s23.text: Now open table three, the response time table, and read the names of the rows carefully.

s24.text: Here is the number everyone quotes. Re reading the whole corpus for every question takes ninety two point zero eight seconds.

s25.text: With the cache precomputed, the same question takes two point two six seconds.

s26.text: Ninety two divided by two point two six is forty point seven. That is where forty times comes from.

s27.text: But look at the name of the ninety two second row. In the published version it says in context learning. In the earlier version, it said without CAG.

s28.text: It is not RAG. It is the model reading the entire corpus again from scratch, on every single question.

s29.text: Now look at the row that actually says RAG. Sparse retrieval, top three passages: zero point zero zero zero eight seconds to retrieve, and zero point six six six seven to generate.

s30.text: Under one second. The cached method takes two point two six.

s31.text: On the paper's own largest test set, plain keyword RAG was three point four times faster than CAG.

s32.text: The forty times speedup is real. It just compares against the slowest possible baseline, not against RAG.

s33.text: What about accuracy? This is where the story gets stranger.

s34.text: The published table two gives CAG a BERT score of zero point seven four zero seven on the large Hot Pot Q A set.

s35.text: Sparse RAG with five passages scores zero point seven five three five. RAG wins that row.

s36.text: But the earlier arXiv version scored CAG at zero point seven five two seven, and marked it as the best result.

s37.text: Same authors, same experiment, two different tables. We checked the source files.

s38.text: In version two, the old table is still in the Latex. It is wrapped in an if false block, so it never appears in the published PDF.

s39.text: The authors also changed the baseline label from without CAG to in context learning, and replaced the old numbers.

s40.text: Articles published after that revision kept quoting the first version. Some still claim CAG was more accurate in every configuration.

s41.text: The honest conclusion is narrower. CAG led on the small and medium sets. On the largest one, the result depends on which version you read.

s42.text: There is a second cost nobody puts in the headline. The cache has to live somewhere.

s43.text: Llama three point one eight billion has thirty two layers, eight key value heads, and one hundred twenty eight dimensions per head.

s44.text: One token needs two values per head, in two byte precision. That is about one hundred twenty eight kilobytes per token.

s45.text: Across eighty five thousand tokens, that is roughly eleven gigabytes of cache, before framework overhead.

s46.text: That is our arithmetic, from the model's published shape, not a figure from the paper.

s47.text: The model weights themselves are about sixteen gigabytes. The cached corpus is most of another model.

s48.text: So is CAG useless? No. It solves a real problem, in a narrow setting.

s49.text: If your knowledge base is small, stable, queried constantly, and does not need different permissions for different people, preloading and caching is a clean design.

s50.text: Internal handbooks, frequently asked questions, support playbooks. The paper names those exact use cases.

s51.text: The authors state the boundary themselves. The method becomes impractical for significantly larger datasets.

s52.text: And they suggest the hybrid. Preload a foundation context, then retrieve only for the edge cases.

s53.text: A recent independent test pushed this to six hundred twenty thousand tokens. CAG stayed accurate, but time to first token rose to about fifteen seconds. Retrieval stayed near one.

s54.text: So the rule of thumb is not which technique wins. It is how much text you are willing to hold in memory for every answer.

s55.text: The paper's own title says, don't do RAG. Its own limitations say when not to do CAG.

s56.text: The next time someone tells you a system is forty times faster, ask what the other row is called.

s57.text: The number was never the lie. The label next to it was.

s58.text: Source: Chan, Chen, Cheng and Huang. Don't do R A G. The Web Conference twenty twenty five, companion proceedings.

s59.text: We read both versions so you do not have to.
